b.answer:
Worked example: Harvest Lane. Tolu's task: sending tomorrow's delivery list to the rider. It happens six evenings a week.

Trigger: 6 p.m. on a delivery day. Outcome: the rider has a complete list of tomorrow's paid orders before 7 p.m. and has replied "OK".

  1. Open the Orders notebook. (notebook)
  2. Find every order for tomorrow's date. (notebook)
  3. Check each order is paid. (bank app)
  4. Copy name, phone, address and items for each paid order. (notebook, WhatsApp Business)
  5. Group the orders by area: Bodija, Mokola, Ring Road. (WhatsApp Business)
  6. Send the list to the rider. (WhatsApp Business)
  7. Confirm the rider replied "OK". (WhatsApp Business)

FRIED: F yes (six times a week). R yes (a new hire could follow the steps above). I mostly: orders are in a notebook today, so this becomes fully digital only once orders live in a sheet. E yes (a missed address means a failed delivery and a refund). D yes. Four and a half of five: a strong candidate.

Note: step 5 is really route planning, which needs local judgement. Keep that one with Tolu and automate the rest.
mistakes: Steps that hide several actions, such as "sort out the orders", instead of one verb + object each.
Naming the first action as the trigger ("open the notebook") instead of the event that starts it (6 p.m., a new message).
Writing the outcome as an activity ("list sent") rather than the result someone cares about (rider has a complete, paid-only list).
Giving a FRIED total with no yes or no per letter, or ticking F for a task that only happens monthly.
b.pass: Five to ten numbered steps, each a single verb + object, with the trigger, outcome and the tool used at every step labelled, and a yes or no for each FRIED letter. A classmate could do the task from the list without asking a question.
b.redo: Send it back if steps are vague or bundled, the trigger or outcome is missing, or FRIED is scored as a number with no reasoning per letter.

s.answer:
Worked example: a fictional hair salon in Enugu (about 60 appointments a week). All runs are per week; the twice-monthly task is converted to 0.5.

TaskRuns/wkMin/runErrorDifficultyWeightedPriority
Send next-day appointment reminders602Med ×1.5Easy ÷1180180
Record transfers in the sales sheet601High ×2Easy ÷1120120
Work out weekly staff commission1120High ×2Medium ÷2240120
Copy WhatsApp bookings into the appointment book601.5High ×2Medium ÷218090
Reorder hair products from supplier (2 a month)0.530Med ×1.5Easy ÷122.523

Top task: appointment reminders (180).

Why it scores high: it runs 60 times a week, and a forgotten reminder means an empty chair the salon can't refill at short notice.

What it depends on: the bookings must already sit in a clean, digital list with name, phone, date and time. Today they live in WhatsApp chats and a paper book, so the reminder can't be automated until task 4 (copying bookings) is solved. That dependency pulls task 4 into the plan even though it ranks fourth.

Input change: replace free-text WhatsApp booking with a short booking form that writes straight into a Bookings sheet. Task 4 then disappears, and the reminders read from the sheet. This is the same move Tolu made with the order form.

Kept manual for now: product reordering. It scores lowest and the owner chooses brands by judgement.
mistakes: Leaving a monthly or daily figure unconverted, so one row is out of scale with the rest.
Multiplying by difficulty instead of dividing, which pushes hard tasks to the top.
Choosing the most annoying task instead of the highest score, then justifying it after the fact.
Justifications that never name a dependency, or leaving the three example rows in the calculator.
s.pass: Five of the learner's own tasks, every row in runs per week, weighted and priority figures that recalculate correctly, and a three-sentence justification for the top task that names at least one dependency and one concrete input change.
s.redo: Send it back for mixed units, maths that doesn't follow runs × minutes × error ÷ difficulty, example rows still present, or a justification with no dependency.

g.answer:
Worked example: a fictional private school in Abeokuta, fee payments. Interview: the bursar, 40 minutes.

Lanes: Parent · Bursar · Class teacher.

  1. Parent: pays fees by transfer, sends a screenshot to the bursar's WhatsApp. Handoff 1 (screenshots get buried in chats).
  2. Bursar: finds the screenshot, checks the bank statement. Decision: amount matches? No → message parent. Yes → continue.
  3. Bursar: writes a receipt in the receipt book, photographs it, sends it to the parent.
  4. Bursar: updates the paper "cleared" list on Friday. Handoff 2 (teachers get it late, so cleared pupils are wrongly turned away).
  5. Teacher: lets cleared pupils sit exams.

Scores (fee season, per week):

StepRuns/wkMinErrorDiff.Priority
Match screenshot to statement803High ×2Medium ÷2240
Write and send receipt802Med ×1.5Easy ÷1240
Update cleared list160High ×2Easy ÷1120
Chase unpaid parents303Med ×1.5Hard ÷345

The case. The first automation is payment confirmation: parents pay through a payment link that signals when money lands, the pupil's row in a Fees sheet changes to Paid, a receipt goes out automatically, and teachers see a live view-only cleared list. Receipts depend on confirmation, so the two top steps are built together. This saves about 460 minutes (7.7 hours) a week in fee season, worth about ₦66,000 a month at ₦2,000 an hour (7.7 × 2,000 × 4.3). Tools start on free plans at this volume; if building takes 15 hours, it pays back within about two weeks. Kept manual: chasing unpaid parents and agreeing payment plans. That is relationship work, so the automation only prepares the list of who owes what.

Submit: the swimlane (photo or Excalidraw), interview notes, the score table and this paragraph.
mistakes: Mapping how the process should work instead of what the person actually does, because they skipped the interview.
Drawing lanes but not circling handoffs, or putting yes/no questions in ordinary boxes instead of diamonds.
A payback estimate with no hourly value or no weekly-to-monthly conversion (× 4.3).
Automating the relationship step (chasing debts, negotiating) instead of keeping it human and preparing the facts for it.
g.pass: A swimlane of a real process with at least two lanes, one decision diamond and at least one circled handoff, a score table, and a one-paragraph case giving weekly hours saved, monthly value with its working, and one named manual step with the reason.
g.redo: Send it back if the map is a single lane or has no decision, there's no evidence of an interview, the payback has no working, or no step is kept manual.
